extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and academic authors preparing books and papers for publication
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for mathematicians on submitting, revising, and producing a mathematics book (from reviews and copyediting through production, marketing, contracts, and royalties). Covers formatting, TeX workflow, backups, and author responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read reviews intensely and dispassionately
rubrics_metrics.description: Read reviews intensely and dispassionately and learn what you can from them; focus on what the reviewer saw when reading the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forget reacting to the criticisms, justifying yourself, answering reviewers’ comments, or becoming emotional. Ask: 'What can I learn from these reviews?' and 'How can I use these comments to improve my book?' There is generally something of value even in the most negative reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect typical review timeline and volume
rubrics_metrics.description: Expect the reviewing process to take three or four months and to see two to four reviews of your work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan your schedule accordingly; publishers will often solicit paid reviewers and then pass anonymous reports to you by e-mail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author bears ultimate responsibility for accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: The reviewer is not responsible for the accuracy and correctness of your work; there is only one person who bears the ultimate responsibility, and that is you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume a favorable review means everything is correct—check every word yourself and certify correctness before final submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the post-review period for substantial rewriting
rubrics_metrics.description: The period immediately following the review process is your last chance for substantial rewriting; treat it as a gift.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take a couple of months to polish the manuscript thoroughly; later you will only have opportunity for small changes in page proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow publisher formatting and submission requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Submit the final, polished draft in the format the publisher requests (often as a *.pdf) and supply source (typically *.tex) when asked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many publishers want manuscripts double or triple spaced to allow copy editors room for markings. Nowadays submission and much of the process is electronic—send *.pdf and *.tex as required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement copy-editor edits in your TeX source
rubrics_metrics.description: When a copy editor sends you edits, you must go into your TeX source file and make the edits yourself (or at least those you agree with).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compile the source to produce a *.pdf and return it to the publisher. The burden of incorporating edits has shifted to the author with TeX and electronic workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyediting consistency and formatting checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Copy editors will check spelling, grammar, syntax, consistency of style, and other nonmathematical aspects of your writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical items include: ensure all displayed equations are formatted the same way; left and right page bottoms align; avoid widows (single line ending a paragraph at top of page) and orphans (single line beginning a paragraph at bottom); position figures properly and render them at correct size; check running heads and page breaks; ensure blank pages at ends of chapters are completely blank. Depending on density of corrections you may be contacted or may have to submit another manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insist on checking title page and back-cover copy
rubrics_metrics.description: Insist on seeing the title page before the book goes to press and review the back cover copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Title page errors (e.g., misspelled name or incorrect affiliation) are embarrassing; back cover copy is important advertising—ensure it says the right things.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the production chain and check repro quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of the production steps (TeX -> DVI -> PostScript -> repro copy -> shooting -> plates -> printing) and their effects on output quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-resolution repro ensures the smallest subscripts and superscripts remain sharp. Modern houses may go directly from electronic files to negatives, skipping repro copy; nevertheless verify rendering at high resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide marketing information and complete the Marketing Questionnaire
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete the publisher’s Marketing Questionnaire carefully and in writing; it is important for pricing, marketing strategy, and advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questionnaire is often long and asks detailed/embarrassing questions (hometown paper, professional societies, ten strongest features, competition, classes where book can be used, enrollment). Editors and marketing rely on this written information—do not attempt to substitute a phone call.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know factors used to estimate market and price
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors estimate sales and price using factors like whether the book is in a hot area, cross-disciplinary interest, student market, author name recognition, and class adoption potential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other considerations: whether it's the first book in a field, competition from established books, and the marketing department’s willingness to promote the book. These influence print run and wholesale price calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiate contract terms prudently
rubrics_metrics.description: Book contracts typically specify royalty rates, deadlines, page lengths, formats (e.g., TeX), and a lot of legal language often slanted toward the publisher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deadlines are negotiable—err on the conservative side (give more time). Negotiate artwork responsibilities, gratis copies, and any provisions you dislike. Most negotiations are pleasant if requests are reasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand standard royalty provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical royalty clauses specify percentage rates (e.g., 10–15% for undergraduate texts), differing treatments for translations, e-books, databases, deep-discount sales, and foreign sales, and exclusions (no royalty on gratis/review copies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contracts define 'Publisher’s net receipts' (sales less discounts, returns, etc.), may allow a reserve for returns, withhold taxes as required, and maintain a Royalty Account charged by advances and author obligations. Royalties on certain rights/sales may be one-half the stated rate. These are negotiable but publishers are careful and explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect publisher control and options in contract
rubrics_metrics.description: Publisher contracts typically give the publisher options (including pulling a project) and many legal provisions favoring the publisher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honorable publishers rarely exercise harsh options but want them available. Familiarize yourself with contract language and negotiate clauses you find unacceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared for production labor and costs even with TeX
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing a reasonably competent TeX file saves money, but copyediting, spacing, consistency, and other production adjustments still cost—Tex reduces but does not eliminate production work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author-supplied TeX reduces typesetting costs ($5k–$7k vs $15k–$20k for traditional typesetting in example), but you must attend to details requested by copy editors and production staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep disciplined versioning and backups
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep every version of your document with clear filenames/timestamps and follow a regular backup routine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use versioned filenames (e.g., TROG.001, TROG.002), leverage file timestamps, and perform regular backups (at least weekly) to external drives or cloud. The 'modified Tower of Hanoi' protocol is recommended for rigorous backups; at minimum, do something systematic—losing your drive is catastrophic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use computer tools to increase productivity but cross-check on paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Computers provide search, cut-and-paste, multiple windows, dictionaries, and easy printing which increases productivity; however, authors should still print drafts for proofreading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electronic workflows prevent interruptions and speed tasks, but printed hard copy and a red pen are valuable for critical reading. Retrain yourself to read typeset output critically since it may look deceptively 'finished.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of differences for college-market textbooks
rubrics_metrics.description: Lower-division college textbooks involve a more collaborative, team-like process in which reviewers and authors may effectively write the book together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such projects are a 'Byzantine tug-of-war' best learned privately; the general remarks about individual-author books may not apply to college-market textbook workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarize yourself with electronic proofreading tools (electronic sticky notes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Copy editors often mark edits on the PDF using 'electronic sticky notes' which become part of the file; authors respond with their own notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn how to view, reply to, and incorporate comments in PDF review workflows; know how to convert the annotated PDF back into revised source and regenerated PDF for resubmission.
